records.text: Unity Catalog OSS keeps track of which tables, volumes, functions, and models exist, where their data lives, and who may use them. Query engines and applications ask it those questions over open REST APIs. The project is hosted by the LF AI & Data Foundation. The project describes itself as "a unified and open governance solution for data and AI assets". That's accurate, but abstract. It's easier to start from the smallest job a catalog has.
records.summary: The open catalog for all your Data and AI assets in the open lakehouse.
records.concepts: Catalog Unity Catalog

records.heading: What a catalog does
records.text: Take a query any data system has to answer: Before reading a single byte, the engine must decide three things. Which files hold the data of my.interesting.table? Is the current user allowed to read them? And what does * expand to, that is, what is the table's schema? Answering those questions has long been the job of the catalog. In a traditional database the catalog is built in and you rarely notice it. The [lakehouse architecture] took that monolith apart: storage and compute became separate systems, and open table formats such as Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg™ took over responsibilities like schema enforcement and ACID transactions. As lakehouses spread, many engines, teams, and AI applications came to share the same storage, and passing file paths around stopped being enough. Readers need to find data by name. Administrators need to decide who may read or change it without handing out storage keys. And the assets worth governing are no longer only tables, but also raw files, functions, and machine-learning models. Unity Catalog provides the catalog as a shared, open service that does these jobs for all of them.

records.heading: What Unity Catalog OSS manages
records.text: Unity Catalog organizes assets in a three-level namespace, catalog.schema.asset. A catalog contains schemas, and a schema contains: Tables. Delta tables, plus other formats registered as external tables. The catalog stores each table's columns, format, and storage location. A managed Delta table goes further: the catalog allocates its storage and coordinates its commits. Views and metric views. Stored SQL or YAML definitions. The catalog keeps the definition, and an engine runs it. Volumes. Governed directories of non-tabular files such as documents, images, or model inputs. Functions. Registered Python or SQL functions, for example as tools for an AI agent. They run in the caller's environment, not on the server. Registered models. MLflow models and their versions, with the catalog as the model registry. Around the namespace the server also manages storage credentials and external locations, which describe the cloud storage it may access, and users, ownership, and privileges, which describe who may do what. For how these objects fit together, see Core concepts.

records.heading: How it works with engines and storage
records.text: Unity Catalog is a metadata and access service. It works alongside the systems that run queries and store data: Engines run the queries. Spark, DuckDB, Trino, Daft, and your own applications connect through the Unity Catalog REST API, the Delta API for catalog-managed Delta tables, or the Iceberg REST API for reading Iceberg tables or Delta tables with Iceberg metadata (UniForm). Storage holds the data. Table and volume files live in object storage or a file system, and the catalog records where. When an engine needs the files, the catalog can issue short-lived credentials scoped to that one table or volume, a mechanism called credential vending. This split is the point of an open catalog. Any engine that speaks the APIs sees the same names, schemas, and permissions, and no engine has to own the data.

records.heading: Governance in the open source server
records.text: With authentication and authorization enabled, the server validates tokens from an external identity provider, maps them to users it knows, and checks ownership and privileges such as USE_CATALOG, SELECT, or MODIFY on every request. Credential vending extends those checks to storage: an engine receives storage access only for data the user may read or write. These checks govern access through the catalog. Anyone holding direct storage credentials can bypass them, so locking down the storage itself remains part of a secure deployment.

records.heading: Unity Catalog OSS and Databricks Unity Catalog
records.text: Databricks created Unity Catalog and open sourced it in 2024. Databricks Unity Catalog is a managed service with the same API heritage and a larger feature set, so a Databricks guide is not automatically a guide for the open source server. These docs describe only the open source server.

records.heading: Define the metric view
records.text: The definition is YAML inside a CREATE VIEW … WITH METRICS statement. Its source names the table. The dimensions are the values you group and filter by, each an expression on a source row. The measures are the aggregations you report: Names can be the ones your reports use, spaces included. Quote them with backticks in queries. The definition starts with version: "0.1", the only version Spark reads.

records.heading: Inspect it

records.heading: Query measures by month
records.text: Wrap each measure in MEASURE() and group by the dimensions you want: Spark turns each MEASURE() into the measure's expression, aggregated over the source rows in each group. The result is what you'd get by writing the GROUP BY against shop.orders yourself. Reading a measure column without MEASURE() fails.

records.text: Filter on one dimension and group by another, or leave out GROUP BY for the total: Revenue per customer over both months is 125.00, not the average of 75.00 and 68.75: four customers spent 500.00 in total. Spark computes each measure from the source rows, never from other results, so a ratio like this one stays right however you slice it.

records.text: You stored three metrics in the catalog and queried them by month, by status, and in total, without repeating their formulas. records.heading: Delete a schema or catalog
records.text: The server rejects a delete while the target still contains objects. It returns HTTP 400 with FAILED_PRECONDITION, and the SDK raises BadRequestException: Python SDK CLI The command exits non-zero, with the message Cannot delete catalog with schemas. Use force=true to force deletion. Delete the contents first, starting with the innermost objects: Python SDK CLI Or delete a catalog with everything in it: Python SDK CLI A forced delete removes every schema, table, volume, function, and model in the catalog, and it can't be undone. The server also deletes the directories of managed tables and volumes, after server.storage-cleanup.initial-delay (7 days by default). External tables and volumes lose only their metadata, and their files stay where they are. Required privileges: to delete a catalog, you need ownership of the catalog or the metastore. To delete a schema, you need ownership of the schema plus USE_CATALOG, or ownership of the catalog or metastore.

records.heading: When to use Delta instead
records.text: Plain files work for data written once and read many times, such as exports and drops from other systems. They lack what a table format adds: No transactions. A reader can see a half-written folder, and two writers can overwrite each other's files. No row-level changes. Updating or deleting rows means rewriting files yourself. No schema enforcement or evolution. Any file in the folder can have any columns. Slower reads at scale. Readers list the folder and read every file's footer or contents to plan a query. Delta keeps file lists and statistics in its log. For data that changes, write Delta and register it, or let Unity Catalog manage the table.

The catalog's record doesn't: its columns, column comments, table comment, and properties all stay as they were registered.

records.heading: Sync the catalog's record
records.text: Send the table's columns, comment, and properties from the Delta log to the catalog in one request to the Unity Catalog Delta API. You send it from Python. If you changed the table in the Spark SQL shell, use the delta-rs · Python tab, which reads the same Delta log: start its session as in Set up the client, and open the table as in Change the Delta log. These two helpers load a table and update it: Then send what your engine reads from the Delta log: Spark · Python delta-rs · Python Load the table again and retry if the server returns HTTP 409 UpdateRequirementConflictException. It means the table changed after you loaded it, and the server applied none of the updates. The Unity Catalog Delta API explains why the server checks requirements and applies updates all or nothing. You can also drop the table from the catalog and register it again, as in Register external Delta table.

records.page: Replace or overwrite a managed Delta table
records.heading: Create a table from a query
records.text: To create a managed table from the result of a query, use CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT without a LOCATION: The new table is catalog-managed, like one made with CREATE TABLE, and its first version, 0, is a CREATE TABLE AS SELECT. It takes its four columns from the query and has no partition columns. Keep USING DELTA. Without it, Spark asks for the session's default format, and the statement fails with Unity Catalog does not support non-Delta managed table.

records.page: Replace or overwrite a managed Delta table
records.heading: Replace a table's definition and rows
records.text: To change a table's columns or partitioning and rewrite its rows in one commit, use CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE … AS SELECT. This statement adds a tax column and partitions the table by day: The new version holds only the query's rows. To get the old rows back, read or restore the earlier version, as in Check a replacement and undo it. The query reads the table it replaces. The result is version 1 of the same table, with the same table ID and location. Version 0 still reads with its old four columns. REPLACE TABLE does the same for a table that must already exist. Use it when replacing a table that isn't there should be an error rather than a new table.

records.page: Replace or overwrite a managed Delta table
records.heading: Overwrite all rows
records.text: To swap every row and keep the table's columns, use INSERT OVERWRITE: The new version holds only the new rows. To get the old rows back, read or restore the earlier version, as in Check a replacement and undo it. The table now holds orders 4, 5, and 6. The new rows must have every column of the table. Two values for this five-column table fail with DELTA_INSERT_COLUMN_ARITY_MISMATCH: target table has 5 column(s) but the inserted data has 2 column(s). To change the columns as well, replace the table instead.

records.page: Replace or overwrite a managed Delta table
records.heading: Overwrite some rows or partitions

records.page: Replace or overwrite a managed Delta table
records.heading: Replace the rows that match a condition
records.text: To replace only the rows that match a condition, use INSERT INTO … REPLACE WHERE. This statement swaps the orders for October 3 for one new order: Order 6, from October 4, stays. Every new row must match the condition. A row outside it fails the whole statement with DELTA_REPLACE_WHERE_MISMATCH, and the table doesn't change.

records.page: Replace or overwrite a managed Delta table
records.heading: Overwrite the partitions the new rows write to
records.text: On a partitioned table, dynamic partition overwrite replaces only the partitions that the new rows land in. Turn it on for the session, run INSERT OVERWRITE, and turn it off again: The new order replaces order 6 in the October 4 partition. Order 7, on October 3, stays. While the setting is on, an INSERT OVERWRITE meant to replace the whole table keeps every partition its rows don't touch, so unset it after the write.

records.page: Replace or overwrite a managed Delta table
records.heading: Check a replacement and undo it
records.text: To see what each statement did, list the table's history: The overwrites are all WRITE operations. The operationParameters column tells them apart: mode is Overwrite for version 2, version 3 records the REPLACE WHERE condition as predicate, and version 4 has isDynamicPartitionOverwrite set to true. To read the table as it was before a change, query an earlier version: To undo a change, restore that version: Restoring commits a new version, 5, whose operation is RESTORE. Versions 3 and 4 stay in the history. Restoring and reading an earlier version need that version's data files. A replacement only marks the old files as removed; VACUUM deletes them once they're older than the table's delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration, 7 days by default. After that, the earlier version can't be read or restored. See Data retention in the Delta docs.

records.page: Replace or overwrite a managed Delta table
records.heading: What a replacement can't change
records.text: A replacement keeps the table's identity. Statements that try to change it fail before they commit, and the table keeps its rows, ID, and history: You try to change What you see The format, for example USING PARQUET Cannot change table format from DELTA to PARQUET The location, with LOCATION cannot specify 'location' or 'external': only catalog-managed Delta tables can be replaced on this path The table ID, with TBLPROPERTIES ('io.unitycatalog.tableId' = …) cannot specify catalog-managed property 'io.unitycatalog.tableId' The catalog-managed feature, with 'delta.feature.catalogManaged' = 'disabled' cannot override 'delta.feature.catalogManaged'='disabled'; expected 'supported' An external table, with CREATE OR REPLACE or REPLACE TABLE REPLACE TABLE is only supported for catalog-managed UC Delta tables; … is EXTERNAL Other table properties aren't protected this way. For example, a replacement with TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableDeletionVectors' = 'false') commits, and the table has deletion vectors off. These statements are verified with Spark. DuckDB can't create a table from a query, and the deltalake-based clients can't open catalog-managed tables.

records.page: Seed TPC-H data into Unity Catalog
records.text: TPC-H is the standard benchmark schema. Its eight related tables model a wholesale supplier: region, nation, supplier, customer, part, partsupp, orders, and lineitem. Seeded into Unity Catalog, it gives you realistic business data to try joins, access grants, and cross-engine queries on. This guide generates TPC-H with DuckDB, writes each table as Delta, and registers it as an external table, three steps per table: generate (DuckDB) → write Delta (deltalake) → register (Unity Catalog) Docker with Compose v2, for the local environment. Unity Catalog 0.7.0, running: Run a local Unity Catalog server. uv. Unity Catalog only records where an external table lives. It never reads the files itself, so the script writes the Delta tables to a local directory it owns. Set TPCH_STORAGE_ROOT to use another directory.

records.heading: Write a definition
records.text: Keep each definition in a YAML file next to your other code, so that changes to a metric go through review like any other change. Spark reads these keys: Key What it holds version "0.1", quoted. Spark rejects other versions. source A table or view name, or a SELECT query. filter Optional. A condition on source rows, applied before every measure. dimensions The values you group and filter by: a name and an expr over a source row. measures The aggregations you report: a name and an aggregate expr. Save this definition as orders_metrics.yaml, in the folder you started Python in. A dimension can be any expression on a row, such as a CASE that turns codes into labels. A measure can combine aggregates, such as revenue divided by the number of distinct customers: Each dimension and measure takes only name and expr. Spark rejects comment, display_name, format, and synonyms, as well as joins and any version but "0.1". To join tables, write the join in the source query, as shown in Compute over a query.

A Unity Catalog volume governs a directory of files that aren't a table: CSV drops, documents, images, model inputs. Like a table, a volume lives in a schema and has a three-level name, such as retail.files.landing. Volumes come in two types: An external volume points at a directory you already have. Unity Catalog records the location and never deletes the files. A managed volume gets a directory that Unity Catalog allocates under the schema's or catalog's storage root. Deleting the volume deletes that directory. For how volumes fit into the namespace, see Core concepts. Docker with Compose v2, for the local environment. Unity Catalog 0.7.0, running: Run a local Unity Catalog server. For managed volumes, a storage root on the schema or its catalog. uv, for the Python examples.

records.heading: Set up the client
records.text: Set up the client for your interface: Python SDK Start Python with the SDK: CLI The examples use a catalog retail with a schema files whose storage root is $UC_DOCS_ROOT/managed: Python SDK CLI

records.heading: Create an external volume
records.text: Point the volume at an existing directory. This example assumes $UC_DOCS_ROOT/landing holds a few files. Python SDK CLI The location must be a directory below a bucket or container root, not the root itself. It must not overlap another table or volume, and it must not contain __unitystorage, the prefix the server uses for managed storage. Required privileges: USE_CATALOG on the catalog (or ownership of it), plus ownership of the schema or USE_SCHEMA and CREATE_VOLUME on it. If the location falls inside an external location, you also need CREATE_EXTERNAL_VOLUME on that external location, or ownership of it.

records.heading: Create a managed volume
records.text: Leave out the location. The server allocates one below the schema's storage root or, if the schema has none, the catalog's. Python SDK CLI The allocated path has the form <storage root>/__unitystorage/schemas/<schema id>/volumes/<volume id>. The server records the path but doesn't create the directory; it appears when the first file is written there. If neither the schema nor the catalog has a storage root, the request fails with None of catalog, schema or storage-root.tables server property has managed location configured. Required privileges: the same as for an external volume, without the external-location check.

records.heading: View volumes
records.text: Python SDK CLI Required privileges: READ_VOLUME or ownership on the volume, plus USE_SCHEMA and USE_CATALOG. Owners of the schema (with USE_CATALOG), the catalog, or the metastore can also view it. A list returns only the volumes you could get.

records.heading: Work with the files
records.text: A volume's metadata tells a client where its files are. The client then reads and writes them with ordinary storage tools. Python SDK With local file:// storage, the location is a directory you can use directly: CLI volume read lists a directory in the volume, or prints a file when --path names one. It runs in the server container. On cloud storage, a client needs credentials for the location. A client with the right privileges can request temporary credentials scoped to a volume from the server; see Credential vending. Open source Unity Catalog doesn't provide the /Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/<volume> paths that Databricks compute mounts. Clients work with the volume's storage_location.

records.heading: Rename or update a volume
records.text: Change the comment, or rename the volume with new_name. Renaming changes only the volume's name. Its files and location stay the same. Python SDK CLI Required privileges: ownership of the volume, plus USE_CATALOG (or ownership) on the catalog and USE_SCHEMA (or ownership) on the schema.

records.heading: Delete a volume
records.text: Python SDK CLI What happens to the files depends on the volume type: Volume type Catalog entry Files External Deleted Left in place. Delete them with your storage tools if you no longer need them. Managed Deleted The server deletes the volume's directory after server.storage-cleanup.initial-delay, 7 days by default. The delay isn't a recovery window: the volume can't be restored, and when the delay passes the files are deleted for good. Copy anything you still need out of the directory first. If a deletion fails, the server retries it after server.storage-cleanup.retry-backoff, an hour by default. Required privileges: ownership of the catalog; or ownership of the schema plus USE_CATALOG; or ownership of the volume plus USE_CATALOG and USE_SCHEMA.

A client that reads or writes data under Unity Catalog asks the server for storage credentials, then talks to object storage itself. Each request names one table, volume, model version, or path, and one operation. The server answers with a short-lived credential for the object's storage that reaches only that object's location and allows only that operation. Engines such as Spark make these requests for you. Make them yourself when you build a client, or open storage from an application. For how the server decides and mints a credential, see Credential vending. Docker with Compose v2, for the local environment. Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with simulated S3 and PostgreSQL, running: Run a local Unity Catalog server. A storage credential and an external location over the data: Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations. uv, for the Python examples, or jq, for the REST examples. The examples use a catalog analytics with an S3 storage root under the external location lake on s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake. Its schema ops holds an external table trips, a managed volume files, and a registered model churn with a finalized version 1.

records.heading: Set up the client
records.text: Python SDK Start Python with the SDK and obstore: Inside async with ApiClient(config) as api:, create the API object: REST API The uc CLI has no command for temporary credentials, so call the REST API: Every response has the same shape: url, the location the credential covers; expiration_time, in epoch milliseconds; and one credential for the storage behind url. For S3 that is aws_temp_credentials, with access_key_id, secret_access_key, and session_token. Azure storage gets azure_user_delegation_sas, with a sas_token, and Google Cloud Storage gets gcp_oauth_token, with an oauth_token.

records.heading: Get credentials for a table
records.text: Look up the table's ID, then ask for READ or READ_WRITE: Python SDK REST API The url is the table's storage location. A READ credential lists and reads the table's files, and S3 rejects its writes. Required privileges: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on the parents, plus SELECT on the table to read, or SELECT and MODIFY to write. Ownership covers each of them (source).

records.heading: Get credentials for a volume
records.text: Look up the volume's ID, then ask for READ_VOLUME or WRITE_VOLUME: Python SDK REST API The url is the volume's storage location. For a managed volume, the server chose it under the schema's or catalog's storage root. Required privileges: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on the parents, plus READ VOLUME to read. Writing needs ownership of the volume (source).

records.heading: Get credentials for a model version
records.text: A model version is named by its model's three-part name and its version number. Ask for READ_MODEL_VERSION to load its files: Python SDK REST API READ_WRITE_MODEL_VERSION works only while the version is PENDING_REGISTRATION, so a client can upload its files. Once the version is finalized, the server refuses with Cannot request read/write credentials on a model version that has been finalized. MLflow makes both requests for you when it registers and loads a model (see Manage models). Required privileges: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on the parents, plus EXECUTE on the registered model to read. Writing needs ownership of the model (source).

records.heading: Get credentials for a path
records.text: Ask for a storage URL directly when no catalog object names it yet, for example to stage files before you register a table: Python SDK REST API The operation is PATH_READ, PATH_READ_WRITE, or PATH_CREATE_TABLE. The credential covers the URL you asked for, not its external location, so ask for the narrowest prefix you need. A URL outside every external location fails with FAILED_PRECONDITION and S3 bucket configuration not found. Required privileges: for a path inside a table, volume, or model, the privileges on that object, as if you had asked for it by name. For a path no object owns, READ FILES on the external location for PATH_READ, or READ FILES and WRITE FILES for PATH_READ_WRITE. PATH_CREATE_TABLE needs CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE on the external location, and the server refuses it for a path that overlaps an existing table, volume, or model. Ownership of the location covers each of them (source).

records.heading: Open storage with the credentials
records.text: Pass the three keys to your S3 client, with the url as its root. With obstore: Python SDK Other S3 clients take the same three values. The AWS CLI and SDKs read them from AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, and AWS_SESSION_TOKEN. S3 rejects any request outside the url, and any write made with a read credential.

records.heading: Renew credentials before they expire
records.text: A long-running client caches a credential until shortly before expiration_time and then asks again. The server checks the grants on every request, so a revoked grant stops the renewal. records.heading: Write a function the catalog can store
records.text: The client builds the stored record from the function's source code, its type hints, and its docstring. Save the function in a module, such as pricing.py in the session's folder: Then import the module into the session: The client reads the source from the module's file. A function with no source file to read, such as one created with exec, fails with OSError: could not get source code.

records.heading: Type hints
records.text: Every parameter and the return value need a type hint. The catalog stores each one as SQL type text: Python type hint Stored type text int LONG float DOUBLE str STRING bool BOOLEAN datetime.date DATE datetime.datetime TIMESTAMP bytes BINARY list[int] ARRAY<LONG> dict[str, int] MAP<STRING, LONG> list ARRAY dict MAP list[str] (return value) ARRAY<STRING> Optional[int] LONG A plain list or dict is accepted, but typing.List with no element type isn't. A parameter gets a stored default only from a Python default: = None is stored as NULL, and = 7 as 7. The client rejects these hints with a ValueError before it sends a request: Union[...], Any, and typing.List with no element type. int | None. Write Optional[int] instead. *args and **kwargs. A parameter with no hint (Missing type hint for parameter: x.) or a return value with no hint. A decimal.Decimal hint fails too, with a pydantic ValidationError.

records.heading: Docstrings
records.text: Write the docstring in Google style. Its description, every paragraph before Args: joined into one line, becomes the function's comment, and each entry under Args: becomes that parameter's comment. A function with no docstring, or with a docstring that has only an Args: section, is rejected with a ValueError. When the Args: entries don't match the signature, the client only issues a UserWarning and registers the function, without comments for the parameters it couldn't match.

records.heading: Imports
records.text: The catalog stores only the function's body, not the module around it. Import what the body needs inside the body, as shipping_cost does with math. A function that uses a module imported at the top of its file registers, but a call returns NameError: name 'math' is not defined as its error.

records.heading: Register a function
records.text: Pass the function, the catalog, and the schema: The function's name in the catalog is its Python name, shipping_cost, under the schema you pass. Required privileges: USE CATALOG on the catalog, or ownership of it. Also USE SCHEMA and CREATE FUNCTION on the schema, or ownership of it. The privileges on this page come from the server's source (FunctionService.java) and haven't been tested against a server with authorization enabled (#282).

records.text: A plain registration stores only the body of the function you pass, so helpers it calls aren't stored. order_total calls apply_discount: If you register it with create_python_function_async, a call to order_total returns a traceback ending in NameError: name 'apply_discount' is not defined as its error. To store the helpers too, register the function with create_wrapped_function_async and list the helpers in functions: The stored body starts with each helper's source, followed by the body of order_total. The name, signature, and comments come from order_total. Required privileges: the same as for registering a function.

records.heading: View a function and get its source back
records.text: Fetch a function by its full name to see what the catalog stores: List the functions in a schema: Print the function as Python source: Or get it back as a Python function you can call in the session: The client rebuilds both from the stored record. The docstring is regenerated, with a Returns: section added, and the parameter defaults are left out. So shipping_cost(2.5), without express, raises a TypeError. Required privileges: one of the following. A call to the function looks it up first, so running it needs the same. Ownership of the metastore or of the function's catalog. Ownership of the function's schema, plus USE CATALOG on its catalog. USE CATALOG on the catalog, USE SCHEMA on the schema, and EXECUTE on the function or ownership of it. Listing returns only the functions you could view this way.

records.heading: Replace a function
records.text: Functions have no update call, so changing a function's body or its comment means replacing it. Registering a name that already exists fails: The message is Function tools.pricing.shipping_cost already exists. Set replace=True to overwrite it. Edit the function in pricing.py: Then reload the module and register the function again with replace=True: A replace deletes the function and creates it again. The new function has a new function_id, and the client that replaced it runs the new body. A replace isn't atomic. If the create fails after the delete, no function is left under the name. For example, the server stores a comment of at most 65,535 characters (FunctionInfoDAO.java), so a replace with a 70,000-character docstring fails with HTTP 500 and the original is gone. Register the function again to restore it. Other clients keep running the old body. A client caches each function the first time it runs it, and a replace from another client doesn't clear that cache. In each application that already ran the function, clear the cache: Required privileges: those for viewing, deleting, and registering a function. The client gets, deletes, then creates the function (client.py), so a replace needs all three.

records.heading: Delete a function
records.text: Delete a function by its full name: After the delete, get_function_async returns None. Required privileges: one of the following. Ownership of the function's catalog. Ownership of the function's schema, plus USE CATALOG on its catalog. USE CATALOG on the catalog, USE SCHEMA on the schema, and ownership of the function.

records.heading: Choose an execution mode
records.text: A client runs functions in sandbox mode unless you create it with execution_mode="local": Any other value raises a ValueError. The two modes differ in where the function runs and what it may do: sandbox (default) local Where the function runs A child process Your process: a sync call on the calling thread, an async call on another thread open and blocked modules Refused Allowed Time and CPU limits Applied Ignored result.error when the function raises The full traceback The exception's message only The sandbox blocks imports of sys, subprocess, ctypes, socket, importlib, pickle, marshal, and shutil (executor_env_vars.py). Local mode runs the body in your process with nothing blocked, so use it only for functions you trust. To see the difference in error text, take a function that raises: Call it in each mode: The sandboxed result ends in ValueError: quantity must be at least 1. The local result holds only quantity must be at least 1. In local mode, from the third call with the same arguments on, the client returns the stored result without running the function. A function with side effects or a time-dependent result returns a stale value. Call client.clear_function_cache(), or create a new client, and the function runs again until the cache fills again.

records.text: In the sandbox, a function can't import a blocked module, and neither can the packages it imports. statistics imports sys, and cloudpickle imports pickle, so a function that imports either fails with The import of module 'sys' is restricted. (or 'pickle'). Import the package in your own code before the call, and the sandboxed function can use it. payload_size imports cloudpickle in its body: Import cloudpickle first, then call it: A function that imports a blocked module itself, such as import sys in its body, still fails. Don't set EXECUTOR_DISALLOWED_MODULES. The client reads any value as a list of single characters, so while the variable is set, the sandbox blocks no module by name.

records.heading: Set time and memory limits
records.text: The sandbox stops a call that runs past its limits. You set them with environment variables, which the client reads on every call: Variable Limits Default EXECUTOR_TIMEOUT Wall-clock time, in seconds 20 EXECUTOR_MAX_CPU_TIME_LIMIT CPU time, in seconds 10 EXECUTOR_MAX_MEMORY_LIMIT Virtual memory, in MB, on Linux only 100 The defaults come from executor_env_vars.py. Local mode ignores the time and CPU limits. To cap a call's wall-clock time, set EXECUTOR_TIMEOUT before the call: The call stops after 3 seconds. result.value is None, and result.error starts with The function execution has timed out and has been canceled. Because the client reads the variable on every call, raising it again lets the same 8-second wait finish. The CPU limit counts seconds of CPU time, not waiting, so a function that sleeps isn't stopped by it. A busy loop is: Set the limit to 1 CPU second and call it: result.error starts with The function execution has been terminated with a signal: signal 9 on Linux, 24 on macOS. The memory limit applies on Linux only. macOS ignores it. On Linux, the 100 MB default is too low for even a small call to succeed, so raise it, as the session command does with EXECUTOR_MAX_MEMORY_LIMIT=4096. The timeout argument of execute_function_async isn't an execution limit. It's the HTTP timeout for fetching the function, so this 2-second call finishes with timeout=0.5:

records.heading: Handle errors
records.text: A call fails in one of two ways: the client raises before the function runs, or the function runs and the result carries an error. The client checks your arguments against the function's registered parameters and raises a ValueError for a wrong type, a missing parameter, or an extra one: A function that doesn't exist, because it was never registered or was deleted, raises AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'input_params'. Anything that goes wrong while the function runs comes back in result.error, with result.value set to None. Check error before you use value. In sandbox mode, its last line is the exception, here from checked_total: Two results need care: A function that returns a falsy value, such as 0, comes back with no error and a notice in value that starts with The function execution has completed, but no output was produced. A function with a list parameter works on the first call. The next call with the same list returns TypeError: unhashable type: 'list' in error. Call client.clear_function_cache() before every call that passes a list.

records.page: Use catalog functions as LangChain tools
records.heading: Control who can call a function
records.text: The toolkit fetches each function from the server when you build a tool, and the client fetches it again on every call (toolkit, client). With authorization enabled, the server returns a function to a caller who (FunctionService.java): owns the metastore or the function's catalog, owns the function's schema and has USE CATALOG on its catalog, or has USE CATALOG on the catalog, USE SCHEMA on the schema, and EXECUTE on the function or owns it. Registering a function needs USE CATALOG on the catalog (or its ownership), plus USE SCHEMA and CREATE FUNCTION on the schema (or its ownership). Creating the catalog needs CREATE CATALOG on the metastore (or its ownership), and creating the schema needs USE CATALOG and CREATE SCHEMA on the catalog (or its ownership). For how these grants inherit, see Core concepts. The function then runs on the agent's machine. By default the client runs it in a sandboxed subprocess, which restricts imports and file access and caps CPU time and memory. It runs inside the agent's own process only if you create the client with execution_mode="local". These rules come from the server's source. These docs haven't run them against a server with authorization enabled.

A registered model in Unity Catalog lives in a schema and has a three-level name, such as unity.manage_models.linear. It holds numbered versions, and each version has its own copy of the model's files in the catalog's managed storage. MLflow's tracking server keeps the runs and the logged models. Unity Catalog keeps the registered models and their versions (how the two services divide the work). On this page, MLflow uploads a version's files and loads them. MLflow, the Python SDK, and the CLI all view, update, and delete models and versions, and only the SDK and the CLI rename them. Each task lists the privileges that the server's authorization rules for models require when authorization is enabled. Docker with Compose v2, for the local environment. A catalog with managed storage, such as unity, and a schema in it, such as unity.manage_models: Manage catalogs and schemas. records.heading: Set up the client
records.text: Set up the client for your interface: MLflow Start Python with MLflow, boto3 for the version's files in S3, and scikit-learn, the library the example model uses: Point MLflow at the tracking server and at Unity Catalog's registry. The uc: prefix on the registry URI selects MLflow's Unity Catalog registry, and AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3 points MLflow at the environment's S3-compatible store. The MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_* settings keep the logged model's files going through the tracking server, whose download links name an address only the environment can reach: Python SDK Start Python with the SDK: CLI The examples use one model, unity.manage_models.linear. The next section registers it with versions 1 and 2, and every section after it starts from there.

records.heading: Register a model version
records.text: Registering needs a model logged in MLflow. To follow along, train two small linear models, y = 2x + 1 and y = 3x + 1, and log each in its own run: The session prints the two logged models' URIs, each of the form models:/m-<id>. Register the first one under the model's name. If the model doesn't exist, MLflow creates it with version 1: MLflow reports: Register the second one under the same name. MLflow adds the next version: Both calls also print a line about waiting for the version and progress bars. One call creates the version, copies the logged model's files into the catalog's managed storage, and marks the version READY. MLflow writes the files with temporary credentials that Unity Catalog issues for that one version. See Credential vending. Version numbers aren't reused. If you delete version 2, the next registration creates version 3. MLflow doesn't pass tags to Unity Catalog. Tags given to register_model or create_registered_model are dropped without an error. Required privileges: mlflow.register_model tries to create the model first and continues only if it already exists, so every call needs all of these: To create the model, even when it exists: USE_CATALOG or ownership on the catalog, and on the schema either ownership, or USE_SCHEMA plus CREATE_MODEL (or CREATE_FUNCTION). Whoever creates the model owns it. To add and finalize the version: ownership of the catalog; or USE_CATALOG and ownership of the schema; or USE_CATALOG, USE_SCHEMA, and ownership of the model. To write the version's files: ownership of the model, plus USE_SCHEMA or ownership on the schema and USE_CATALOG or ownership on the catalog. Owning the catalog doesn't replace owning the model.

records.heading: View models and versions
records.text: MLflow Search takes no filter_string or order_by for models, and no order_by for versions. Either one raises Argument '…' is unsupported for models in the Unity Catalog. Python SDK CLI A version's status is READY once registration finishes. Its source is the logged model it was copied from, models:/m-<id>. Its run_id is set only when you register from a runs:/<run-id>/<path> URI. A model's storage_location is a directory in the catalog's managed storage, and each version's files sit below it, under versions/. Required privileges: one of ownership of the metastore; ownership of the catalog; USE_CATALOG and ownership of the schema; or EXECUTE or ownership on the model, plus USE_SCHEMA and USE_CATALOG. A list of models returns only the models you could get.

records.heading: Load a model version
records.text: Load a version by its number, and get the location of its files: The session prints the version's signature, with the input column x as a double, then the prediction [21.], since version 1 fits y = 2x + 1. The signature comes from the version's files, not from Unity Catalog's record of the version. The location has the form s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/unity/__unitystorage/catalogs/<id>/models/<id>/versions/<id>. MLflow reads the files with read-only credentials from Unity Catalog. Load by number only. Unity Catalog's registry has no aliases and no stages, so models:/<name>@<alias> and models:/<name>/latest raise NotImplementedError: Method not implemented. So do setting an alias, get_latest_versions, and transition_model_version_stage. Required privileges: the privileges to view the version, and to read its files, EXECUTE or ownership on the model, plus USE_SCHEMA or ownership on the schema and USE_CATALOG or ownership on the catalog. Owning the catalog or the metastore doesn't replace these.

records.heading: Update comments
records.text: Besides the model's name, a comment is the only metadata you can change on a model or a version. Set one on the model and one on version 2: MLflow MLflow calls the comment description: Python SDK CLI The Python sessions echo the updated model and version. Other versions keep their comments. Models and versions have no tags: set_registered_model_tag and set_model_version_tag raise NotImplementedError. A version's signature and input example live in its files, not in Unity Catalog. Required privileges: one of ownership of the catalog; USE_CATALOG and ownership of the schema; or USE_CATALOG, USE_SCHEMA, and ownership of the model. The same holds for a model's comment and a version's.

records.heading: Rename a model
records.text: Rename a model with the Python SDK or the CLI. new_name is the model's name within its schema. MLflow's rename_registered_model raises NotImplementedError. The example renames the model to linear_regression and prints the result, then renames it back, so the examples below still find it as linear: Python SDK CLI The model keeps its id, storage location, comment, and versions. Only its name changes. Required privileges: the same as for updating a comment.

records.heading: Delete versions and models
records.text: Required privileges: to delete a version, or a model with or without force, the same as for updating a comment.

records.heading: Delete a version
records.text: MLflow Python SDK CLI

records.heading: Delete a model
records.text: A model that still has versions is deleted only with force. Without it, the server refuses with Unable to delete a registered model with existing model versions. The Python SDK and the CLI pass force. MLflow can't, so its example deletes the versions first, a page of search results at a time, until none are left: MLflow Python SDK When you're done, close the client: CLI

records.heading: What happens to the files
records.text: The catalog entry goes at once. A background worker in the server deletes the version's or the model's directory in managed storage no sooner than server.storage-cleanup.initial-delay after the delete, 7 days by default, and retries a deletion that fails. The run and the logged model on the MLflow tracking server, with their files, stay. The delay isn't a recovery window: a deleted model or version can't be restored, and once the worker runs its files are gone for good. Load or copy anything you still need first.

Its artifact name carries the Spark version, and it needs a Delta Spark build for the same Spark version: Spark Unity Catalog connector Delta Spark 4.1 (tested here: PySpark 4.1.0) io.unitycatalog:unitycatalog-spark_4.1_2.13:0.7.0 io.delta:delta-spark_4.1_2.13:4.3.1 4.0 io.unitycatalog:unitycatalog-spark_4.0_2.13:0.7.0 io.delta:delta-spark_4.0_2.13:4.3.1 4.2 (tested here: PySpark 4.2.0, in Working with metric views) io.unitycatalog:unitycatalog-spark_4.2_2.13:0.7.0 io.delta:delta-spark_4.2_2.13:4.4.1 With a Delta Spark release older than 4.3.0, the connector quietly skips the Delta API, and catalog-managed tables don't work.

records.heading: Configure the session
records.text: Register the catalog under a Spark catalog name and point it at the server. The Spark name is your choice. Using the Unity Catalog catalog's own name, here unity, keeps three-part names the same in Spark and in the catalog: Each setting has a job: Setting Purpose spark.jars.packages Downloads the connector and Delta Spark. spark.sql.extensions, spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog Enable Delta's SQL support in the session. spark.sql.catalog.<name> Registers the Unity Catalog catalog <name> with Spark. Repeat this block for each catalog you use. spark.sql.catalog.<name>.uri The server's base URL, without /api/2.1/unity-catalog. spark.sql.catalog.<name>.auth.* How Spark authenticates. See the next section. spark.sql.defaultCatalog Lets queries leave out the catalog name. The same keys work as --conf options for spark-submit, spark-sql, and pyspark, with --packages in place of spark.jars.packages. If you reach Maven through a mirror, add .config("spark.jars.repositories", "https://<your-mirror>") to the builder.

records.heading: Authenticate to the server
records.text: The connector always needs an authentication type, even when the server has authorization disabled. Without one, the first query fails with Required configuration key 'type' is missing or empty. Static token. Set auth.type to static and auth.token to a Unity Catalog access token. The local server above accepts any value. Older configurations set token instead, which still works. Set only one of the two. OAuth client credentials. Set auth.type to oauth, plus auth.oauth.uri, auth.oauth.clientId, and auth.oauth.clientSecret. auth.oauth.scope defaults to all-apis. The connector fetches and renews the token itself. This page doesn't test the OAuth flow. Keep secrets out of source code. Read the token or client secret from the environment or a secret store when you build the session.

records.heading: Check the connection
records.text: List the catalog's schemas and the tables in one of them: The sample catalog's default schema lists tables such as numbers and marksheet. These sample tables live inside the server's container, so this local Spark can list them but can't read their files. Create your own tables under a storage root that both sides can reach, as in Create and update a catalog-managed Delta table.

records.heading: Tune storage credentials
records.text: When Spark reads or writes a table, the connector asks the server for short-lived storage credentials for that table's location. It applies them per table. Three catalog options control this, and the defaults suit most setups: Option Default Effect renewCredential.enabled true Fetches new credentials before vended ones expire, so long jobs keep running. credScopedFs.enabled true Caches file-system clients per credential, not per bucket, so tables in the same bucket don't share access. deltaRestApi.enabled true Uses the Delta API for Delta tables. Catalog-managed tables need it. Set them like the others, for example spark.sql.catalog.unity.renewCredential.enabled. For how the server decides what each credential may access, see Credential vending. Option names and defaults come from the connector source, OptionsUtil.java and AuthConfigs.java.

records.text: Create a secret that holds the server's address and a token, then attach one Unity Catalog catalog as a DuckDB database: ENDPOINT is the server's base URL, without /api/2.1/unity-catalog. records.heading: Query a table
records.text: Use three-part names, or just the table name for tables in the default schema: DuckDB asks the server for the table's location and for temporary credentials, then reads the Delta files directly from storage. For a catalog-managed table it reads the latest version the server has accepted. DuckDB reads tables with column mapping through Unity Catalog, too.

records.heading: Append rows
records.text: INSERT adds rows to the table: On a catalog-managed table, DuckDB writes the new data and commit file, then asks the server to accept the commit as the table's next version. From then on, Spark and every other client see the new rows. DuckDB can't append to a partitioned table that uses column mapping. The insert fails with Not implemented Error: Inserting into a partitioned Delta table that uses column mapping is not supported, and the table doesn't change.

records.heading: Create, change, and drop tables
records.text: CREATE TABLE creates a catalog-managed table, and INSERT adds its rows: The server stages the new table as it does for Spark, so Spark and other clients read it and append to it. DuckDB can't create a table from a query (CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT), update or delete rows, or drop a table. Do those with Spark, as in Create and update a catalog-managed Delta table.

records.heading: Required privileges
records.text: With authorization enabled, reading needs USE CATALOG on the catalog, USE SCHEMA on the schema, and SELECT on the table. Appending also needs MODIFY on the table, and creating a table needs CREATE TABLE on the schema. Owners have all of these. See Core concepts.

records.heading: How Iceberg names map to the catalog
records.text: Every client is configured with the same three values: Iceberg REST setting Value Catalog URI http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog/iceberg Warehouse The name of one Unity Catalog catalog, here retail. A client works with one catalog at a time; configure a second client catalog for another. Token A Unity Catalog access token, sent as a bearer token. The local server has authorization disabled and accepts any value. Inside that catalog, an Iceberg namespace is a Unity Catalog schema, and an Iceberg table is a table whose data source format is ICEBERG. Namespaces don't nest. A table created without a location is a managed table under the schema's or catalog's storage root; the server records where it lives and deletes its files when you drop it. Through this API, the server lists Iceberg tables, and Delta tables only when they carry UniForm Iceberg metadata. Reach other Delta tables with a Delta client, or with both in one Spark session.

records.heading: Write and read rows
records.text: Spark DuckDB PyIceberg DataFusion The client writes data and metadata files with the vended credentials, then asks the server to commit the new snapshot. The server accepts a commit only if the table hasn't changed since the client read it, so concurrent writers can't overwrite each other.

records.page: Use Iceberg REST clients with Unity Catalog
records.heading: Update and delete rows
records.text: Spark UPDATE, DELETE FROM, and MERGE INTO need the Iceberg SQL extensions from the session configuration. DuckDB PyIceberg PyIceberg has no UPDATE. Replace the matching rows with overwrite and an overwrite_filter. DataFusion DataFusion's Iceberg integration has no UPDATE or DELETE FROM; its INSERT INTO only appends.

records.page: Use Iceberg REST clients with Unity Catalog
records.heading: Rename and drop a table
records.text: Spark DuckDB PyIceberg DataFusion DataFusion SQL has no ALTER TABLE … RENAME, so rename through the catalog. DataFusion keeps the table names it has already seen, so drop the renamed table through the catalog too, or create the provider again before you name it in SQL. A rename keeps the table in its schema. Dropping a managed table removes it from the catalog, and a background worker on the server deletes its files. An external table, one created with an explicit location, keeps its files; the server accepts a purge request for it but leaves the files in place. Only tables created through Iceberg REST can be dropped through it. Drop a Delta table through Spark's Unity Catalog connector or the Unity Catalog API.

records.heading: Join Delta and Iceberg tables in Spark
records.text: One Spark session can hold both kinds of table: register the catalog twice, once through the Unity Catalog connector for Delta tables and once through Iceberg REST for Iceberg tables. records.heading: Add the dependency

records.page: Use the Java client in an application
records.heading: Connect to the server
records.text: Build one ApiClient and create the API classes from it. Java has no interactive shell, so put this and the following steps in your application's main method or service setup: uri is the server's address only. The builder appends the API's base path, /api/2.1/unity-catalog. The builder requires a token provider. A server with authorization disabled, such as the docs' local one, doesn't check the token, so any value works there. For a server with authorization enabled, pass a token the server issued. For OAuth client credentials, call TokenProvider.create with type set to oauth, plus oauth.uri, oauth.clientId, and oauth.clientSecret. The provider gets the token and renews it 30 seconds before it expires. oauth.scope defaults to all-apis. addAppVersion adds your application's name and version to the User-Agent header the client sends. The client retries a request up to three times in all, with exponential backoff from 500 ms and random jitter, when the server returns HTTP 429 or the connection fails or times out. It doesn't retry other errors. To change that, pass .retryPolicy(JitterDelayRetryPolicy.builder().maxAttempts(5).build()) to the builder.

records.text: The server reads etc/conf/hibernate.properties, relative to its working directory. In the container that's /home/unitycatalog/etc/conf/hibernate.properties. Replace the file with one that names your database: Key What it sets hibernate.connection.driver_class The JDBC driver. org.postgresql.Driver ships in the image. hibernate.connection.url The JDBC URL. Keep it: the server has no separate schema migration tool. hibernate.archive.autodetection, hibernate.show_sql The image's defaults. The file replaces the image's own hibernate.properties, so write all of these keys, not only the ones you change. With Docker, bind-mount it read-only over the path above. On Kubernetes, mount it from a Secret, because it holds the password. Then restart the server. If you run the server from a release tarball or a source build instead of the image, also put the PostgreSQL JDBC driver on the server's classpath, as the upstream deployment guide describes. A server that can't reach the database doesn't start. It exits with Exception during creation of SessionFactory and the database's reason, for example FATAL: password authentication failed for user "unitycatalog". A server whose server.properties sets server.env=test ignores hibernate.properties and keeps its metadata in memory. Use dev or leave it unset.

records.page: Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations
records.text: A Unity Catalog server governs access to Amazon S3 through storage credentials and external locations, and it never hands out long-lived keys. When an authorized client needs data, the server assumes an IAM role through AWS STS and returns credentials that expire after an hour and are scoped to the path the client asked for. For why this matters, see Credential vending. Three IAM principals and two catalog objects are involved: Name on this page What it is Where it lives Master role uc-master The identity the server runs as. It may only assume storage roles. IAM, attached to the server's host Storage role uc-storage-lake Reads and writes one bucket or prefix. It trusts the master role. IAM Storage credential lake_storage Records the storage role's ARN, plus an external ID that the server generates. Unity Catalog External location lake Binds s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake to the storage credential. Unity Catalog When a client requests access to a path under s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake, the server finds the matching external location, assumes its credential's storage role as the master role with the credential's external ID, and attaches a session policy that narrows access to the requested path and operation. Docker with Compose v2, for the local environment. Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with simulated S3 and PostgreSQL, running: Run a local Unity Catalog server. In AWS, permission to create IAM roles and policies, and to edit the bucket's policy if it has one. uv, for the Python examples. To try the steps without an AWS account, use the local environment above with simulated S3. It runs the server's real AWS code path, but it doesn't check trust policies or external IDs, so do the IAM steps for real on AWS.

records.page: Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations
records.heading: Set up the client
records.text: Set up the client for your interface: Python SDK Start Python with the SDK: Create the API objects from an open client: async with ApiClient(config) as api: credentials = CredentialsApi(api). CLI The CLI connects to http://localhost:8080 by default. Pass --server and --auth_token to reach a different server.

records.page: Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations
records.heading: Run the server as a master role
records.text: Create an IAM role for the server, for example uc-master, with a permission policy that allows only sts:AssumeRole on your storage roles. A name prefix keeps the policy stable as you add storage roles: Attach the role to wherever the server runs: an EC2 instance profile, an ECS task role, or an EKS service account through IRSA or EKS Pod Identity. Then set the role's ARN and region in server.properties: Leave aws.accessKey and aws.secretKey unset. The server then signs its STS calls through the AWS SDK's default credential chain, which picks up the attached role. aws.masterRoleArn doesn't select an identity. The server reports it to whoever creates a storage credential, as the principal that the storage role must trust, so it must match the role the server actually runs as. The server reads each key from a JVM system property first, then from an environment variable with the same name (for example aws.region), then from server.properties. If aws.region is unset, the server uses the AWS SDK's region chain, then the global STS endpoint. Use exactly these key names. The aws.s3.masterRoleArn-style spellings in the upstream docs/server/aws.md are silently ignored by the server.

records.page: Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations
records.heading: Run outside AWS
records.text: On premises, prefer IAM Roles Anywhere: it gives the host temporary credentials for the master role through the same default credential chain, so the configuration above doesn't change. If that isn't possible, use an IAM user as the master identity. Grant it the same policy, set aws.masterRoleArn to the user's ARN, and pass its keys in aws.accessKey and aws.secretKey (or the standard AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY variables). The local stack does this, with its simulated S3 keys.

records.page: Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations
records.heading: Create a storage credential
records.text: First create the storage role in IAM, for example uc-storage-lake. Give it a permission policy on the bucket and prefix it serves. A temporary trust policy is enough for now; you replace it once the server has generated the external ID. The server narrows each vended credential to object reads (s3:GetO*) and prefix-scoped s3:ListBucket, or for writes, also s3:PutO*, s3:DeleteO*, and the multipart actions. Actions the storage role lacks stay denied, so grant everything your engines need. Engines such as Spark may also call s3:GetBucketLocation. Then register the role with Unity Catalog: Python SDK CLI The response's aws_iam_role holds three values: role_arn (the storage role), unity_catalog_iam_arn (the server's aws.masterRoleArn), and external_id, a UUID the server generated for this credential. Required privileges: ownership of the metastore, or CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL on it.

records.page: Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations
records.heading: Update the storage role's trust policy
records.text: Replace the storage role's trust policy so that only the master role can assume it, and only with this credential's external ID. The external ID stops another tenant of the same server from pointing their own credential at your role. Substitute unity_catalog_iam_arn for the principal and external_id for EXTERNAL_ID_FROM_THE_CREDENTIAL. If the master identity is an IAM user, use the user's ARN as the principal.

records.page: Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations
records.heading: Create an external location
records.text: An external location makes the server use the credential for every path under its URL: Python SDK CLI External locations can't overlap. The server rejects a URL that equals, contains, or falls inside another external location's URL, with Cannot accept an external location that duplicates or overlaps with existing external location. Use one location per prefix that has its own storage role. Required privileges: ownership of the metastore; or CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on the metastore plus ownership of, or CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on, the storage credential.

records.page: Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations
records.heading: Check that the server vends credentials
records.text: Ask for temporary credentials on a path under the location. A successful response proves the whole chain: the server's identity, the trust policy, the external ID, and the storage role's access. Python SDK The example writes and lists a file with the vended keys: CLI The uc CLI has no command for this, so call the REST API: To use the keys with the AWS CLI, export access_key_id, secret_access_key, and session_token as AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, and AWS_SESSION_TOKEN. The credentials reach only the requested path. A write to s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake/curated with keys vended for s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake/landing is denied. If the request fails with AccessDenied from STS, check the trust policy and the external ID first. Tables and volumes use the same mechanism. Their credential endpoints resolve the object's storage location to its external location. Required privileges: for a path that no table, volume, or registered model owns, ownership of the metastore or of the external location, or READ FILES on the location (PATH_READ) or both READ FILES and WRITE FILES (PATH_READ_WRITE). For a path inside a table or volume, the usual privileges on that object apply instead, such as SELECT on a table or READ VOLUME on a volume.

records.page: Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations
records.heading: View storage credentials and external locations
records.text: Python SDK CLI The CLI's credential and external_location commands take the flags --name, --aws_iam_role_arn, --url, --credential_name, --comment, --new_name, and --force. Their --help pages crash. Required privileges: ownership of the metastore, or ownership of (or CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on) the credential. For an external location: ownership, or any of READ FILES, WRITE FILES, CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE, CREATE EXTERNAL VOLUME, and CREATE MANAGED STORAGE on it.

records.page: Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations
records.heading: Update a credential or external location
records.text: To move a credential to a different storage role, update its role ARN: Python SDK CLI Changing the role ARN generates a new external_id. Vending fails until the new storage role's trust policy names the new ID. Update the trust policy right after the credential. A comment or name change keeps the ID. Update an external location's comment, name, credential, or URL the same way: Python SDK CLI The server doesn't check what lives under a location before it accepts a new URL. Tables, volumes, and managed storage roots under the old URL lose their credential, and vending for them fails with FAILED_PRECONDITION. Before you change a URL, create the new location alongside the old one if the prefixes don't overlap, and move the data first. Required privileges: for a credential, ownership of it or of the metastore. For an external location, ownership of the metastore, or ownership of the location plus ownership of (or CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on) any new credential.

records.page: Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations
records.heading: Delete an external location and credential
records.text: Delete the location first, then the credential: Python SDK CLI An external location can't be deleted while a table, volume, or registered model is stored under it. Catalog and schema storage roots don't count. A credential can't be deleted while an external location uses it. force skips these checks. Deleting either object removes only the catalog entry. The data in S3 and the IAM roles stay. Always delete the location before its credential. Force-deleting a credential that a location still uses breaks every list of external locations. To recover, force-delete the location by name: uc external_location delete --name <name> --force true. Required privileges: ownership of the object or of the metastore.

The Delta API is a versioned REST interface that Unity Catalog serves under /api/2.1/unity-catalog/delta/v1/, next to the Unity Catalog REST API's /tables endpoints. A Delta client uses it to stage, create, load, and commit to a catalog-managed Delta table. External tables and catalog-managed Delta tables walks through that lifecycle. This page explains why each part of the API is designed the way it is. The diagram follows one table through the API, from negotiation to its first commit. Expand it to step through each call: This page's script, delta_api_semantics.py, sends the requests shown here to a server and checks the responses the page describes.
records.summary: Unity Catalog's Delta API applies requirements and updates all or nothing, and carries Delta's own schema and table features on the wire.
records.concepts: Unity Catalog (OSS) Unity Catalog Delta Lake Delta Spark Table Storage credential issuer

records.heading: One endpoint takes requirements and updates
records.text: A commit proposal and every metadata change to a table go to one endpoint, POST …/tables/{table}, as a list of preconditions (requirements) and a list of intents (updates). Dropping and renaming a table have endpoints of their own. The server checks every requirement, then applies every update, or applies none. A request that sets a comment and a property looks like this: The same envelope carries a new commit (add-commit), a schema change, a protocol upgrade, and a property change. They can share one request, so a change and the commit that writes it land together or not at all. All or nothing extends to a request the server rejects as malformed. A request may carry at most one update of each action type, add-commit included, and at most one requirement of each type (spec, delta.yaml). The file actions a writer repeats, Delta's add and remove, aren't actions in this API. They live in the commit file that the one add-commit names, and a commit file holds as many as the commit needs. A set-properties and a remove-properties that touch the same key are rejected rather than applied in order. The order of entries in either list carries no meaning, because the server applies actions in a fixed order of its own (spec). When the server rejects one, none of its valid updates apply either, and the table's etag stays the same.

records.heading: Negotiation comes first
records.text: Before any other request, a client asks GET /delta/v1/config with a catalog and the protocol-versions it supports. Both parameters are required, and a missing one is a 400. The answer names a protocol version and the endpoints the server offers for it: The endpoints come back as strings, and clients route by them instead of building paths. The strings carry the resolved catalog name, warehouse here, while the schema and table segments stay templates. That design leaves room to change the API: The version lives in each returned path (/v1/…), so a later protocol version can lay out its paths however it needs. A server may list endpoints beyond the specification's. Clients ignore strings they don't recognize, so a new endpoint doesn't break an old client. The specification treats a 404 on config as a server that doesn't support the protocol, and tells the client to fall back to the Unity Catalog table APIs. An unknown catalog is also a 404. Its error type, NoSuchCatalogException, tells the two apart. The specification defines a negotiation: the client offers the highest version it supports per major version, and the server picks the highest version both support. The Unity Catalog server doesn't negotiate. It ignores protocol-versions and answers 1.0 whatever the client offers, even 2.0 alone. Check that the returned protocol-version is one you offered. Treat any other answer as an unsupported server, as the specification does for a 400. config covers the protocol version and its endpoints, not table features. The catalog states those when a table is staged.

records.heading: The catalog sets table features at staging
records.text: When a client stages a table, the catalog states the Delta protocol the table must use: a required protocol and properties, and a suggested protocol and properties. Condensed, the server's answer reads: The required protocol is reader version 3 and writer version 7. Its reader and writer features are catalogManaged, v2Checkpoint, vacuumProtocolCheck, and deletionVectors, and the writer features add inCommitTimestamp. The required properties include io.unitycatalog.tableId, which equals the staging table's ID. A null value means the engine generates the value. The catalog asks for column mapping in name mode but leaves delta.columnMapping.maxColumnId to the engine that assigns the column IDs. The catalog names the property, and the engine, which knows the schema, fills it in. The response is authoritative. The specification's list of features is a non-normative reference, and the specification lets a catalog grow or shrink the set. Clients read the response fields rather than hard-coding a list. A catalog that serves a stateful compaction service, for example, may require domainMetadata so that the service's state is kept with the table. Unity Catalog OSS ships a fixed set, defined in UcManagedDeltaContract.java. When the client then creates the table, the server checks the declared protocol and properties against the managed-table contract. The staging response also carries one READ_WRITE credential whose prefix is the table's location, so the engine can write version 0 without standing access to the bucket. Credential vending explains that trust boundary.

records.heading: Optimistic concurrency with assert-table-uuid and assert-etag
records.text: The API doesn't lock tables. A writer loads the table, prepares its change, and states in requirements what it assumed when it loaded: assert-table-uuid is required on every request. A request without it is a 400 (assert-table-uuid requirement is required). Names get reused: a table can be dropped and created again under the same name. UUIDs don't, so the assertion stops a change meant for the old table from landing on the new one. assert-etag is optional. The etag is an opaque token from loadTable. If the table has changed since, the server answers 409 UpdateRequirementConflictException and applies nothing: An add-commit for version v also asserts, without saying so, that the table is at version v-1. Commits go in order, one version at a time: after a Spark INSERT, the table's latest version is one higher, and its newest commit carries that version. When another writer has already taken the version, the specification defines a second 409, CommitVersionConflictException. So a 409 comes in two kinds: the version was taken, or a requirement failed. Either way, the change didn't land.

records.heading: Retry or rebase
records.text: The two kinds of failure call for different responses. The specification's commit recovery rules say: On a 5xx or a timeout, resend the identical request. The outcome is unknown, and the server deduplicates a retry by the staged commit's file name. A byte-for-byte retry resolves to what happened the first time. Rebase only once you know the attempt didn't land. A 409 tells you, and so does a reload that shows another writer's commit at the proposed version. Rebasing means building the commit again against the reloaded state, with a new commit file. Rebasing while the outcome is unknown can commit the same change twice. Abort if the reloaded UUID differs. The table was dropped and created again under the same name, so the change no longer has a target.

records.heading: Metadata changes travel with add-commit
records.text: A catalog-managed table has two views of its metadata: the catalog's record and the Delta log. The API keeps them in lockstep with one rule. A change that the Delta log also represents, such as the schema, the protocol, or a delta.* property, goes in the same request as the add-commit whose commit file writes it. A change that lives only in the catalog, such as the table comment, may go alone. Engines follow the rule: after a Spark ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMNS, the table's version is one higher, and both the Delta API and the Unity Catalog REST API list the new column. The rule falls on the client. The specification doesn't require the server to inspect staged commit files (spec), so clients can't rely on it to check that declared metadata matches the commit file, and they own the consistency of the two views. If the two views diverge anyway, the Delta log wins for snapshots: engines rebuild the table from its commits, and the catalog's record serves discovery. The server accepts a log-represented change with no commit. A set-properties that turns delta.enableDeletionVectors off on a managed table succeeds without a new version, and the Delta log keeps the old value. The specification calls such a request a client error. Don't rely on the server to catch it: send log-represented changes only with the add-commit that writes them. An external table has no add-commit, because the catalog doesn't accept its commits. Its sync is metadata-only: the client sends what it reads from the Delta log to the catalog's record, as in Sync the catalog's record.

records.heading: Delta's own schema on the wire
records.text: The Delta API sends a table's columns as a Delta struct type, the same shape as metaData.schemaString in the Delta log. Column-mapping metadata travels with each field: The protocol travels the same way, as reader and writer features. Nothing is translated: an engine gets the schema in the shape it writes to the log, with the column IDs and physical names it assigned. Compare the Unity Catalog REST API, which describes each column as a ColumnInfo with type_name, type_text, and type_json. That shape serves every format the catalog registers. The Delta API serves only Delta tables, so it uses Delta's own shapes.

records.heading: Further reading
records.text: External tables and catalog-managed Delta tables walks through the lifecycle of a catalog-managed table. Credential vending explains the credentials the staging and table responses carry. Manage schemas and properties uses the Delta API to sync an external table's record. The managed Delta tables specification defines the protocol, and the Delta API definition defines every endpoint and field. The Delta protocol defines catalog-managed tables from the table's side.

Unity Catalog is a registry of named objects. Each object has an owner and a set of grants that decide who can use it, and most objects describe files that live somewhere else. The umbrella term for these objects is securable. This page follows the order in which a catalog is built up: the namespace that names every asset; catalog administration: the metastore, catalogs, and schemas, and the credentials and external locations that let the server reach storage; the data and AI assets that users, pipelines, and agents work with; how those objects relate to the files they describe; the privileges the server checks on each object; the users those privileges are granted to.
