records.heading: The three-level namespace
records.text: Assets are addressed by a three-part name, catalog.schema.object: Names are unique within their parent: two schemas may both contain an orders table, but their full names differ. Clients refer to assets by full name and never need to know where the files are. Storage credentials and external locations sit outside the namespace. They have single-part names and are addressed by name alone.

records.heading: Metastore, catalogs, and schemas
records.text: The metastore is the top-level container. An open source server has exactly one. It has an ID (GET /metastore_summary) but no name, and it never appears in object names. Privileges that aren't tied to a catalog, such as creating catalogs, are granted on the metastore. A catalog is the first level of the namespace. Teams typically use catalogs to separate business units, environments, or data products. A schema sits inside one catalog and groups related assets. Every asset belongs to exactly one schema.

records.heading: External data access
records.text: Two kinds of object live directly under the metastore and hold no data. They decide which storage the server can reach, and on whose behalf. A storage credential holds the cloud identity the server uses to reach storage. In this release every credential has the purpose STORAGE, and the credential service implements AWS IAM roles. Azure and Google Cloud access are configured on the server rather than as credential objects. An external location pairs a storage path, such as s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/retail/, with a storage credential. It doesn't have to be a bucket root. A location can cover any path prefix, and narrower locations give narrower control. External locations decide who may create external tables and volumes under a path, use it as managed storage, or read and write its files directly. With these objects in place, the server can hand out short-lived credentials scoped to a single asset or path. It exposes one endpoint each for tables, volumes, model versions, and raw paths. See Credential vending.

records.heading: Managed storage roots
records.text: The metastore, a catalog, and a schema can each declare a storage_root. When the server creates a managed object, it takes the location from the nearest root: the schema's storage_root, if it has one; otherwise the catalog's storage_root; otherwise the metastore's storage_root. The server allocates a unique path below that root, under a reserved __unitystorage prefix, for example <root>/__unitystorage/schemas/<schema id>/volumes/<volume id>. External objects may not use paths containing __unitystorage.

records.heading: Data and AI assets
records.text: Every asset lives in a schema. The securable type is the name the permissions API uses for the object. Object Securable type What it describes Table table Tabular data with a column schema and a format, such as Delta or Parquet. Its table type says who manages it: EXTERNAL or MANAGED. SQL views (VIEW) and metric views (METRIC_VIEW) are stored as table types too, with a definition instead of a storage location. Volume volume A directory of non-tabular files, either EXTERNAL or MANAGED. Function function A registered routine with typed parameters and a body. The catalog stores the definition, and the caller's environment runs it. Registered model registered_model A named ML model with numbered model versions. Each version has its own storage location for its artifacts. Versions aren't securables of their own: privileges on the model cover them. A managed Delta table starts life as a staging table: the server reserves a location, the client writes the first commit there, and creating the table ratifies it. See External tables and catalog-managed Delta tables. A view holds no data. The catalog stores its definition, and the engine that queries it runs that definition. See SQL views and metric views as catalog objects. The API's TableType enum also lists STREAMING_TABLE and MATERIALIZED_VIEW. An enum value is not the same as a supported workflow, so check the release's compatibility notes before relying on those types.

records.heading: Objects versus files
records.text: A catalog object and the files it describes are separate things. Unity Catalog stores names, columns, comments, and a location. The files sit in object storage or on a local disk. Three consequences follow. Renaming moves nothing. Renaming a schema or a volume changes its catalog name only. The files stay at the same location, and clients that look the object up by name find it under the new name. External and managed decide who owns the files. For an external table or volume, you supply the location and keep control of its lifecycle. Dropping the object deletes only the catalog entry. For a managed table or volume, the server allocates the location below a storage root and treats the files as part of the object. Dropping it deletes them too, once a cleanup delay passes (7 days by default). One file, one object. An external table or volume may not overlap another one's location, so any one file is governed by a single object. The catalog doesn't stand between a client and storage. A client that can reach the files directly, through its own cloud credentials or a shared disk, can read them without asking Unity Catalog. To make the catalog the gatekeeper, withhold direct storage access and have clients request temporary, scoped credentials from the server.

records.heading: Ownership and privileges
records.text: The server checks privileges only when authorization is enabled (server.authorization=enable in server.properties). With it disabled, every request is allowed. Every securable has an owner. The principal that creates an object becomes its owner. OWNER is the only privilege that implies the others: the owner can read, modify, drop, and grant privileges on the object. The server has no ALL PRIVILEGES, MANAGE, or BROWSE. The server's checks honor ownership on the way down: the owner of a catalog can manage every schema and asset in it, and the owner of a schema can manage every asset in that schema. The metastore owner is the server's administrator. Other principals need privileges. The server checks each privilege on a specific object type: Checked on Privileges Metastore CREATE CATALOG, CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION, CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL Catalog USE CATALOG, CREATE SCHEMA Schema USE SCHEMA, CREATE TABLE, CREATE VOLUME, CREATE FUNCTION, CREATE MODEL Table SELECT, MODIFY Volume READ VOLUME Function, registered model EXECUTE Storage credential CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION External location CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE, CREATE EXTERNAL VOLUME, CREATE MANAGED STORAGE, READ FILES, WRITE FILES Access to an asset also needs access to its parents. Reading a table takes SELECT on the table, USE SCHEMA on its schema, and USE CATALOG on its catalog. Writing to it takes both SELECT and MODIFY. USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA don't grant access to anything inside on their own. They let a principal reach the objects it holds other privileges on. Creating an object works the same way: a CREATE … privilege on the parent, plus USE on every level above it. Privileges other than OWNER are inherited. A privilege granted on a catalog or schema also applies to every object below it, so SELECT on a schema covers every table in it, including tables created later. OWNER applies only to the object it's held on. Grants are read and changed through the permissions API, which addresses an object by its securable type and full name (/permissions/{securable_type}/{full_name}). A change adds or removes privileges for one principal. The CLI wraps the same calls in bin/uc permission create | get | delete. The how-to guides list the privileges each operation needs, for example Manage catalogs and schemas and Manage volumes.

records.heading: Principals and users
records.text: A principal in the open source server is a user, identified by email address. The server has no groups or service principals, so every grant names an individual user. The server keeps its own user list, managed through a SCIM 2.0 Users API under /api/1.0/unity-control/scim2/Users (create, list, get, update, delete) and /scim2/Me for the calling user. The CLI wraps it as bin/uc user. A user record holds a display name, an email address, an optional external ID, and an active flag. Users authenticate with an identity provider, such as Google, then exchange that provider's token for a Unity Catalog token at /auth/tokens. The exchange succeeds only for an active user that is already registered on the server. Registration and grants are two separate steps: a new user can sign in but reaches nothing until someone grants them privileges. On first start with authorization enabled, the server creates an admin user, makes it the metastore owner, and writes a token for it to etc/conf/token.txt. That account is the bootstrap: use it to register the first real users and grant them access. This page describes the open source server's behavior, based on its API definitions and authorization source. Databricks Unity Catalog adds securables and governance features beyond it, so a Databricks guide may not apply here.

records.text: Unity Catalog knows two kinds of table. They differ in two things: who owns the files, and who decides which version of the table is the current one. This page explains both kinds, what the server does for a catalog-managed Delta table, and which engines can use each kind.

records.page: External tables and catalog-managed Delta tables
records.heading: Two questions decide the kind
records.text: Who owns the files? An external table points at a location that someone else chose and controls. The catalog records the table's name, columns, format, and location, and never moves or deletes the files. A managed table lives at a location the catalog chooses, under the storage root of its schema or catalog. The catalog creates that location, and deletes it when the table is dropped. Who decides the latest version? A Delta table is a series of numbered commits in its _delta_log. For an external table, the files decide: whichever writer manages to put commit file N in place first has made version N, and the catalog plays no part. For a catalog-managed Delta table, the catalog decides. A writer proposes commit N, and it becomes the table's version N only once the server accepts it. In Unity Catalog the two answers go together. Managed tables are always Delta, and a client that creates one through the Delta API, such as Spark with Delta 4.3 or later, makes it catalog-managed. External tables never are. records.page: External tables and catalog-managed Delta tables
records.heading: Why a catalog should accept commits
records.text: When the files decide, the storage system has to resolve races between writers, and every guarantee follows from that one atomic file operation. That has worked for years, but it leaves the catalog as a bystander. The catalog can't reject a commit that breaks a rule, can't see a commit before it lands, and can't coordinate changes across tables. When the catalog accepts commits, it becomes the table's source of truth. Two writers that race for the same version get one acceptance and one rejection, whatever the storage system offers. The catalog can require table features, such as deletion vectors or in-commit timestamps, before a table may exist. A reader asks the catalog for the latest version instead of listing files. Delta records this arrangement in the table itself as the catalogManaged table feature. The Delta protocol requires every client that reads or writes such a table to ask the catalog.

records.page: External tables and catalog-managed Delta tables
records.heading: The lifecycle through the Delta API
records.text: The server speaks to Delta clients through the Delta API, a versioned REST interface under /api/2.1/unity-catalog/delta/v1/. Its managed-tables protocol defines each step. Expand the diagram and step through it: The lifecycle has four parts. Negotiate. The client asks GET /delta/v1/config which endpoints and which protocol version the server supports. The server answers with the endpoints it implements and protocol version 1.0. Stage. To create a table, the client asks for a staging table. The server picks the location, issues a read-write credential for it, and states the Delta protocol the table must use. The server answers like this: The response also lists the matching required and suggested table properties. The client writes version 0 of the Delta log at that location, then asks the server to turn the staging table into a real one. Commit. For each change, the client writes the new data files and a commit file under _delta_log/_staged_commits/, named with the version and a random ID. It then sends one request that names the commit and the conditions under which to accept it, for example that the table is still the one it loaded. The server checks the conditions and accepts or rejects the commit as a whole. Load. A reader asks the server for the table. The response includes the latest accepted version and the recent commits, so the reader knows exactly which files make up the table. Throughout, the server hands out storage credentials scoped to the table's location, so no client needs standing access to the whole bucket. See Credential vending for that trust boundary.

records.page: External tables and catalog-managed Delta tables
records.heading: What clients must support
records.text: Because the protocol lives in the table, a client that doesn't speak it can't use the table at all, not even to read it. Unity Catalog gives a path-based client nothing to work with: delta-rs 1.6.6, pointed at a managed table's location, stops with Max catalog version is required when loading a catalog-managed table. That refusal is deliberate. A client that only lists files could miss commits the catalog has accepted, or write a version the catalog never approved. So for a managed table, choose a client that goes through the catalog. These include Spark with the Unity Catalog connector and Delta 4.3 or later, and DuckDB's unity_catalog extension for reads and appends. An external table makes the opposite trade. Any client with access to the storage can read and write it, including tools that have never heard of Unity Catalog. That suits data that another system already owns. But the catalog can't coordinate those writers, and its record of the columns can fall out of step with the files. records.heading: When to use which
records.text: Use a managed table when Unity Catalog should own the data. You get a location nobody has to plan, commits that the catalog checks, and clean deletion. Use an external table when the data already exists, when another system writes it, or when it isn't in Delta format. Registering such a table gives it a governed name without changing who writes it.

Engines read and write a lakehouse's data directly in object storage, so something has to give them access to that storage. With credential vending, the Unity Catalog server gives it. The server holds the one identity that can reach the storage. A client proves who it is to the catalog and asks for access to a single table, volume, model version, or path. If the catalog's grants allow it, the server returns a credential that works only for that location and that kind of access, and that expires within an hour. This page explains how that exchange works and where its guarantees end.
records.summary: How Unity Catalog issues short-lived storage credentials scoped to one table, volume, or path, and why that makes the catalog the gatekeeper for data access.

records.heading: Why vend credentials instead of sharing keys
records.text: The alternative is to give every engine and user a storage key, or to keep a bucket policy for each of them. Each key is a standing secret that can leak. It usually reaches far more data than its holder needs. Revoking access means rotating the key everywhere it was copied, and the catalog's grants and the storage's permissions drift apart. Vending moves the long-lived secret into one place, the catalog server, and gives clients only short-lived, narrow credentials. That has three effects: Clients prove identity and never hold long-lived keys. A client authenticates to the catalog with its own token. The storage identity never leaves the server. Each credential has a small blast radius. It covers one location and one operation, so a leaked credential exposes one table's files for at most an hour. Grants take effect quickly. Every credential request passes the catalog's authorization check. Revoke a grant and the next request fails. The longest delay is the remaining lifetime of a credential already handed out. No key needs rotating. The catalog makes the access decision, and the storage enforces it on every request. Neither has to trust the client.

records.heading: The flow
records.text: A client that reads a table makes two calls to the catalog before it touches storage. Expand the diagram and step through it: Resolve. The client looks up the table by name with its own bearer token. The answer includes the table's ID and its storage location. Request. The client asks POST /temporary-table-credentials for that table ID and an operation, READ or READ_WRITE. Authorize. The server checks the caller's privileges. A read needs USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, and SELECT on the table. A write also needs MODIFY. Ownership covers both. If the check fails, no credential is minted. Mint. The server finds the external location that contains the table's path and uses that location's storage credential. It asks the cloud's credential issuer for a credential narrowed to the table's location and the requested operation. Return. The client receives the credential, the URL it covers, and an expiration_time in epoch milliseconds. Read. The client reads the files straight from storage. Data never flows through the catalog. The storage rejects any request outside the credential's scope. Renew. Before the credential expires, a long-running client asks again, and the server checks the grants again. Volumes, model versions, and paths follow the same flow through their own endpoints.

records.heading: What a credential covers
records.text: The server vends credentials through four endpoints. Each request names one object and one operation, and the privileges it needs depend on both. A request for anything inside a schema also needs USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on its parents, or ownership of them. Endpoint Operations Privileges required /temporary-table-credentials READ, READ_WRITE SELECT to read; SELECT and MODIFY to write; or ownership /temporary-volume-credentials READ_VOLUME, WRITE_VOLUME READ VOLUME to read; ownership to write /temporary-model-version-credentials READ_MODEL_VERSION, READ_WRITE_MODEL_VERSION EXECUTE on the registered model to read; ownership to write /temporary-path-credentials PATH_READ, PATH_READ_WRITE, PATH_CREATE_TABLE The privileges of the object that owns the path. For a path no object owns: READ FILES on the external location to read, READ FILES and WRITE FILES to write, CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE to create a table, or ownership A path request can't get around a table's grants. If the path falls inside a table or volume, the server applies that object's privileges, as if the client had asked for the object itself. Engines that speak the Delta API get credentials from its own endpoints, with the same checks. When a client creates a catalog-managed table, the staging response already includes a read-write credential for the new table's location. The Iceberg REST API returns a credential with each table it loads, plus the endpoint the client calls to renew it before it expires.

records.heading: How the server mints a credential
records.text: The server never stores credentials for individual tables. It works them out when asked. The table's storage location falls under exactly one external location, which names a storage credential, which holds the identity the server uses with the cloud. External locations can't overlap, so the answer is always unique. See Core concepts for how locations and storage roots fit together. Each cloud narrows the credential differently: Storage How the credential is narrowed What the client receives Amazon S3 The server calls AWS STS AssumeRole on the storage role, with a session policy that allows only the requested prefix and operation. Access key, secret key, and session token, valid for one hour Azure Data Lake Storage The server gets a user-delegation key from the storage account and signs a SAS token for the requested path. A user-delegation SAS, valid for one hour Google Cloud Storage Google STS downscopes the server's token with a credential access boundary on the requested prefix. An OAuth token Storage credentials as catalog objects exist for AWS only. Azure and GCS vending uses server-wide adls.* and gcs.* settings in server.properties, and so does S3 when no external location covers a bucket. For the AWS setup (master role, storage roles, external IDs), see Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations. A file:// location needs no keys. The server still checks the privileges, but its answer carries only the location. That is why local examples print empty credentials.

records.heading: Expiry and renewal
records.text: A credential expires on its own. Its response carries expiration_time in epoch milliseconds. Clients should cache the credential until shortly before then and request a new one, rather than ask again for every file. The Spark connector does this automatically with its renewCredential.enabled option (see Configure Spark). If you build your own client, give its storage layer a credential callback that asks the catalog again before expiry. obstore's credential providers, for example, cache a credential until the expires_at you return. The server can't recall a credential it has already issued. Revoking a grant stops new credentials, but an existing one stays valid until it expires.

records.heading: Where the trust boundary sits
records.text: Vending protects data only if the catalog is the only way to reach it. These are the places where that assumption ends: Standing storage access bypasses the catalog. Anyone who can reach the bucket with their own IAM role or key never asks the catalog, so its grants don't apply to them. Keep direct access to governed locations limited to the server's identity and to operators. A vended credential is a bearer credential. Storage doesn't know who it was vended to. Whoever holds it can use it until it expires, so treat it like any other secret in logs and job configuration. Access is all-or-nothing per location. A credential opens every file under the table's location. The catalog can't use it to hide rows or columns, because the client reads the files itself. Row filters and column masks need an engine you trust to apply them. The decision is only as strong as authentication. With authorization disabled, the server vends to any caller. Enable authentication and authorization before you point the server at real storage. The server's identity is the crown jewel. The master role, or the keys in server.properties, can reach every governed location. Protect the server host and its configuration accordingly.

Set managed storage for catalogs and schemas on S3 puts managed tables and volumes under an external location. Read files from a volume requests a volume credential and opens storage with it. records.page: How Unity Catalog and MLflow divide responsibilities
records.text: With Unity Catalog as MLflow's registry, a model involves two services. MLflow records how the model was made. Unity Catalog holds the registered model, such as unity.model_split.linear, and its numbered versions. The two services never share a record. A version points back at MLflow by URI, and registering copies the model's files into the catalog's storage. So each side keeps working when the other side's copy is deleted.
records.summary: MLflow tracks experiments, runs, and logged models. Unity Catalog registers the model, numbers its versions, stores their files, and governs access.

records.page: How Unity Catalog and MLflow divide responsibilities
records.heading: What MLflow tracks
records.text: MLflow keeps the training side of the model. An experiment groups runs. A run records its parameters, such as fit_intercept, and its metrics, such as r2. When the training code calls log_model, MLflow creates a logged model with a URI of the form models:/m-<id>. A logged model has its own identity. It belongs to a run when you log it inside an active run, and otherwise it has no run (model.py). The logged model holds the files that a later load needs, such as the MLmodel descriptor and the serialized model. All of this lives in MLflow's own stores, not in the catalog. The tracking server writes runs and logged-model metadata to its backend database, and serves the logged model's files from its artifact store through URIs that start with mlflow-artifacts:/.

records.page: How Unity Catalog and MLflow divide responsibilities
records.heading: What Unity Catalog registers
records.text: Unity Catalog keeps the governed side of the model: the registered model, its versions, their files, and who may use them. A registered model lives in a schema next to tables, volumes, and functions, and has a three-level name, catalog.schema.model. Each registration adds a version with the next number: 1, 2, 3. A version records its status, a storage_location for its files, and two links back to MLflow. source holds the logged model's URI, models:/m-<id>. run_id holds the run's ID when you register from a runs:/<run-id>/<path> URI, and stays empty when you register from models:/m-<id>. The server chooses a registered model's storage when the model is created. It uses the schema's managed storage, or the catalog's if the schema has none (ModelRepository.java, ExternalLocationUtils.java). If neither has managed storage, creating the model fails. Each version then gets its own folder under the model's location. In the uc-mlflow environment, a version of a model in the unity catalog lands at s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/unity/__unitystorage/catalogs/<id>/models/<id>/versions/<id>. A registered model is a securable, so the privilege model applies to it when authorization is enabled. The uc-mlflow environment runs with authorization disabled. Creating a model takes CREATE MODEL on the schema. Using one takes EXECUTE on the model, plus USE SCHEMA on its schema and USE CATALOG on its catalog. Versions aren't securables of their own: the privileges on the model cover every version.

records.page: How Unity Catalog and MLflow divide responsibilities
records.heading: Where each piece is stored
records.text: In the uc-mlflow environment, both services share one PostgreSQL server and one object store, but each keeps to its own database and its own bucket: Object Owned by Metadata Files Experiment and run, with parameters and metrics MLflow mlflow database — Logged model, models:/m-<id> MLflow mlflow database mlflow bucket, served by the tracking server Registered model Unity Catalog unitycatalog database — Model version Unity Catalog unitycatalog database amzn-s3-demo-bucket bucket, under the model's location Because each side keeps its own records and files, each survives the other's deletes. Deleting a model's versions and then the model in Unity Catalog leaves the run active, with its parameters and its logged model's files. Deleting the run, the logged model, and the logged model's files in MLflow leaves the version READY, and it still loads from Unity Catalog's storage.

records.page: How Unity Catalog and MLflow divide responsibilities
records.heading: What registering a model version does
records.text: Registering a model version copies the logged model's files into a new version, in four steps that the MLflow client drives (create_model_version): Create. The client downloads the logged model's files from the tracking server and asks Unity Catalog to create the version, sending its source and run_id. The server assigns the version number and a storage location, and the version starts as PENDING_REGISTRATION. Get credentials. The client asks Unity Catalog for temporary credentials with the READ_WRITE_MODEL_VERSION operation, scoped to that version's location (uc_oss_rest_store.py). Credential vending explains how the server mints them. Upload. The client writes the files to the version's location with those credentials. Finalize. The client tells Unity Catalog the upload is done, and the version becomes READY. MLflow's client reaches Unity Catalog when its registry URI is uc:<server URL>, such as uc:http://localhost:8080. MLflow takes the server from the URI and a bearer token, if any, from the MLFLOW_UC_OSS_TOKEN environment variable (oss_registry_utils.py). The tracking URI stays separate: the Unity Catalog store has no tracking URI of its own, so runs and logged models stay on the tracking server. The logged model and its files stay in MLflow's store. Loading models:/<catalog>.<schema>.<model>/<version> reads the version's copy from Unity Catalog's storage, not from MLflow's.

records.page: How Unity Catalog and MLflow divide responsibilities
records.heading: What the registry doesn't do
records.text: Unity Catalog's registry, and MLflow's store for it, leave out several features that other MLflow registries have: No aliases or stages. MLflow refuses to set aliases or move versions between stages, so models:/<name>@<alias> and models:/<name>/latest don't resolve. Load a version by its number instead. No tags. MLflow refuses to set tags on models and versions, and drops tags passed when registering without an error. No rename through MLflow. The Python SDK and the CLI rename a registered model. No serving. Registering deploys nothing, and loading runs the model in the loading process. Manage registered models shows the error each of these raises.

records.page: SQL views and metric views as catalog objects
records.text: In Unity Catalog, a view is a catalog entry with a table type and a stored definition. It has no storage location and holds no data. When you query it, a query engine reads the definition from the catalog, expands it in its own dialect, and runs it against the source tables. A metric view is the same kind of entry, but its definition declares measures and dimensions in YAML instead of a query.
records.summary: Unity Catalog stores a view's definition, columns, and dependencies, and the engine runs it. A metric view's definition is YAML with measures and dimensions.
records.concepts: Metric view Query engine Unity Catalog (OSS) Apache Spark View

records.page: SQL views and metric views as catalog objects
records.heading: What the catalog stores for a view
records.text: A view is stored as a table entry, so it's listed with the schema's tables and uses the same API. These fields set it apart: Field SQL view Metric view table_type VIEW METRIC_VIEW view_definition The query text after AS, as written The YAML, as written columns The output columns and their types The dimensions and measures, as columns view_dependencies The tables the query reads, if known The tables the YAML reads, at least one storage_location Empty Empty When it creates a view, the server checks the request's shape: there's a definition, at least one column, and every listed dependency exists (TableRepository). It stores the definition as sent. Spark sends the query text after AS with its line breaks and indentation. The server never parses a view's definition. A VIEW whose definition is the text this is not a query registers without error and is stored unchanged. The error comes later, from the engine that tries to run it. When Spark creates a view, it also stores properties on the entry: the session's current catalog and namespace, the schema mode, the output column names, and the session's SQL settings, so it can read the view back the same way. Registering a view through the REST API generates none of these, so the entry holds only the properties the client sends. To register a view without Spark, see Manage SQL views.

records.page: SQL views and metric views as catalog objects
records.heading: Where a view runs
records.text: The engine that reads a view runs it. It fetches the stored definition, parses it in its own SQL dialect, and plans the expanded query as if you had typed it. So a view's definition only works in engines that understand its dialect. A client that only talks to the REST API can store and return a definition, but it can't run one, and the Iceberg REST catalog serves no views. For a SQL view, Spark works out the dependencies from the query as best it can. A view over samples.views_explained.orders records that table. A view with no source table, such as SELECT 1 AS one, records an empty list.

records.page: SQL views and metric views as catalog objects
records.heading: SQL views versus metric views
records.text: Both kinds are stored definitions that an engine expands at query time. They differ in what the definition holds and how you query it: SQL view Metric view Definition A SQL query YAML version 0.1: a source, optional filter, dimensions, and measures A query returns The query's rows Measures aggregated over the dimensions you group by How you query it SELECT its columns like a table SELECT dimensions, wrap each measure in MEASURE(), and GROUP BY Dependencies Optional At least one, or the server rejects it Use a SQL view to name a query: a join, a filter, or a renamed set of columns that several readers share. Use a metric view when the thing to share is a calculation, such as revenue or order count. Its readers then pick the grouping at query time, and every query computes the measure the same way. A metric view over the orders table with a Revenue measure of SUM(amount) returns revenue per status when you group by Status, and the grand total when you don't. To work with each kind, see Manage SQL views and Manage metric views.

records.page: SQL views and metric views as catalog objects
records.heading: Changing a stored definition
records.text: The server checks a view once, when it's created. Dropping a source table later leaves the view listed, with view_dependencies still naming that table. Only a query against the view fails. The stored columns are checked only at read time too: they're a contract the engine plans against, and the server doesn't compare them with the query. Because the catalog can't update a view, a change means dropping it and creating it again, and the new entry gets the same checks. For the steps, see Change or rename a view and Change a metric view's definition.

records.page: SQL views and metric views as catalog objects
records.heading: Permissions
records.text: Because a view is a table entry, the server applies the table rules to it. These rules come from the server's source, linked at v0.7.0. The server has no row filters or column masks to attach to a view. For the privilege model itself, see Ownership and privileges. Create a view: the same privileges as creating a table. You need USE CATALOG on the catalog, or to own it, and you need either ownership of the schema or USE SCHEMA and CREATE TABLE on it (CREATE_TABLE). Read a view's entry: USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, and ownership, SELECT, or MODIFY on the view. The catalog's owner can read it too, and so can the schema's owner with USE CATALOG (GET_TABLE, TableService). Listing a schema's tables returns only the views and tables you can read. When a view is created, the server checks that its dependencies exist, not that the creator can read them (TableRepository). Reading the view's entry gives the engine the definition. Going by the server's source (TableService), the engine then reads each source table as the caller, so a view doesn't hide its source tables: a reader needs access to them as well.
